## Introduction

Marine aquaculture has the potential to be an important source of protein, with lower environmental costs than many land-based meat production systems (Hall et al., 2011). Gentry et al. (2017) mapped the global potential for marine aquaculture and found that current global seafood demand could be met using only a small fraction of suitable ocean area. In this analysis, I identify which Exclusive Economic Zones (EEZs) on the U.S. West Coast are best suited for aquaculture based on each species' sea surface temperature and depth requirements. I first develop the workflow for oysters, then turn it into a reusable function and apply it to red abalone. I chose red abalone because a few of my friends work at the abalone farm in the Goleta/Gaviota area. They've explained to me how different foods cause the different colors in the shell. So, they're relevant to my personal life, but also the greater Santa Barbara and Channel Islands area. 


## Prepare Data

I need to load the necessary packages and data to get started. The data I'm working with consists of NOAA’s 5km Daily Global Satellite Sea Surface Temperature Anomaly v3.1 (SST), SeaLifeBase information on oysters and red abalone, the General Bathymetric Chart of the Oceans (GEBCO), and designating maritime boundaries using Exclusive Economic Zones (EEZ) off of the west coast of US from Marineregions.org. Here, I also loaded and stacked the SST rasters that were between 2008 and 2012. 

```{r}
# LOADING PACKAGES
library(tidyverse)
library(sf)
library(here)
library(tmap)
library(terra)
```

```{r}
# READING IN THE DATA
# Read in the West Coast EEZ boundaries
eez <- st_read(here("data", "wc_regions_clean.shp"), quiet = TRUE)

# Read in the bathymetry raster
depth <- rast(here("data", "depth.tif"))

# Read in and stack the SST rasters (2008–2012)
sst_files <- list.files(here("data"), pattern = "average_annual_sst", full.names = TRUE)
sst <- rast(sst_files)
names(sst) <- paste0("sst_", 2008:2012)

# Check that all 5 years loaded
if (nlyr(sst) != 5) {
  stop("Expected 5 SST layers (2008–2012), but found ", nlyr(sst))
}
```

After reading in the data, I need to check if the coordinate reference system's (CRS) match. If they don't I need to transform them so that they do match. 

```{r}
# Look at the CRS of each dataset
crs(sst, describe = TRUE)
crs(depth, describe = TRUE)
st_crs(eez)$input
# They all use WGS 84

# Reproject depth to match SST if needed
if (!same.crs(depth, sst)) {
  warning("Depth CRS does not match SST. Reprojecting depth to match SST.")
  depth <- project(depth, crs(sst))
} # No warning was printed

# Transform EEZ to match SST if needed
if (!same.crs(sst, st_crs(eez)$wkt)) {
  warning("EEZ CRS does not match SST. Transforming EEZ to match SST.")
  eez <- st_transform(eez, crs = crs(sst))
} # No warning was printed

# Confirm everything matches before moving on
if (same.crs(depth, sst) & same.crs(sst, st_crs(eez)$wkt)) {
  print("All datasets share the same CRS.")
} else {
  stop("CRS mismatch remains between datasets.")
}
```

All of the datasets share the same CRS, so there was no need to transform any of them. I placed warnings in the code that would run if the CRSs didn't match. 


## 1. Process Data

First, I average the five SST layers into one layer to simplify things. It creates a single raster of average SST. 

```{r}
# 1a. Average the 5 SST layers into one layer
sst_mean <- mean(sst, na.rm = TRUE)
sst_mean
```

Then, I convert average SST from Kelvin to Celsius so that it's more relevant. I also ran a summary of the raster to look at the minimum, median, maximum, and number of NA's. 

```{r}
# 1b. Convert Kelvin to Celsius 
sst_mean_c <- sst_mean - 273.15
sst_mean_c
```

```{r}
# The summary function takes a sample of the raster
summary(sst_mean_c)
```

Here, the minimum value is around 7ºC, median is 14ºC, maximum is almost 33ºC, and there are 41,907 NA values. 

```{r}
# The global function provides the real min, max, and mean of the raster
global(sst_mean_c, fun = c("min", "max", "mean"), na.rm = TRUE)
```

Using the `global` function, the minimum comes out to be around 5ºC, the maximum is still almost 33ºC, and the mean is a little more than 14ºC. 

After converting to Celsius and looking at the summary statistics, I crop the depth raster to match the extent of the SST raster. 

```{r}
# 1c. Crop depth to the SST extent
depth_crop <- crop(depth, sst_mean_c)
```

Now, the resolutions of the SST and depth data do not match. So, I have to resample the depth data to match the resolution of the SST data using the bilinear method approach. 

```{r}
# 1d. Resample depth to the SST resolution
depth_resamp <- project(depth_crop, sst_mean_c, method = 'bilinear')
```

I check each version of the `depth` raster to make sure the changes I've been making have been working. `depth_resamp` should match the resolution and extent of `sst_mean_c` to continue with the analysis. 

```{r}
# 1e. Check that they line up
# Printing each raster to check the resolution, extent, and CRS
print(depth)
print(depth_crop)
print(depth_resamp)
print(sst_mean_c)
```

The resolution and extent match, so now I will double check that everything matches with `compareGeom()`.

```{r}
# Check that the extent, resolution, and CRS match
compareGeom(depth_resamp, sst_mean_c)
```


## 2. Find Suitable Locations

Now that the data has been processed and everything matches, I can move further into the analysis. To find suitable locations for marine aquaculture, I'll need to find locations that are suitable in terms of both SST and depth.

I need to reclassify SST and depth data into locations that are suitable for oysters. To do this, I set suitable values to `1` and unsuitable values to `NA`. 

```{r}
# 2a. Oyster SST range: 11–30°C
rcl_sst <- matrix(c(-Inf,  11, NA,   # colder than 11°C → not suitable
                       11, 30,  1,   # 11–30°C → suitable
                      30, Inf, NA),  # warmer than 30°C → not suitable
                  ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE)

sst_suit <- classify(sst_mean_c, rcl_sst, include.lowest = TRUE)
```

This area includes the entire ocean surrounding the West Coast because it's data on sea surface temperature that happens to be in the range needed for oyster development. 

```{r}
# Oyster depth range: 0-70 m
rcl_depth <- matrix(c(-Inf, -70, NA,   # deeper than 70 m → not suitable
                       -70, 0,  1,     # 0 to 70 m deep → suitable
                       0, Inf, NA),    # above sea level (land) → not suitable
                    ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE)

depth_suit <- classify(depth_resamp, rcl_depth, include.lowest = TRUE)
```

This area includes the depth ranges that are suitable for oysters. Most of the ocean in this extent falls within the oysters’ 11–30°C range, while the 0–70 m depth range only covers a thin strip near the coast. 

The next step is to combine the two rasters so that both the correct SST and depth are in one place. 

```{r}
# 2b. Combine them so only cells meeting BOTH are kept
suitable <- lapp(c(sst_suit, depth_suit), fun = function(x, y) {x * y})
```

This area includes the regions of the West Coast that are suitable for oyster growth and development. The minimal area along the coast from `rcl_depth` became even smaller when the SST and depth were combined together. There's only a few locations that are suitable for oysters. 


## Determine the Most Suitable EEZ

I want to determine the total suitable area within each Exclusive Economic Zone in order to rank zones by priority. To do so, I need to find the total area of suitable locations within each EEZ. 

The first step is to select suitable cells within West Coast EEZs. Before I can do that, I have to turn the EEZ polygons into a raster. 

```{r}
eez_rast <- rasterize(eez, suitable, field = 'rgn')
plot(eez_rast, main = "West Coast EEZs",
     xlab = "Longitude", ylab = "Latitude", legend = FALSE)
```

The plot shows the West Coast ocean split up into five colored regions. The regions include Washington, Oregon, and Northern, Central, and Southern California. 

Now, I can keep only the suitable cells within the EEZs.

```{r}
# 3a. Keep only suitable cells inside the EEZs
suitable_eez <- mask(suitable, eez_rast)
plot(suitable_eez, main = "Suitable cells for oysters within West Coast EEZs",
     xlab = "Longitude", ylab = "Latitude", legend = FALSE, col = "darkgreen")
```

This plot shows a dark green, thin line around the coast that consist of the suitable areas for oysters both regarding sea surface temperature and depth. The area only includes the three states on the West Coast of the lower 48 states. The area is a thin line because the depth is shallower by the coast than in the open ocean. 

The next step is to find the area of each grid cell. 

```{r}
# 3b. Get the area of each cell
suitable_area <- suitable_eez * cellSize(suitable_eez, unit = 'km')
suitable_area
```

Now that each cell's area has been found, I can find the total suitable area within each EEZ. 

```{r}
# 3c. Add up suitable area in each region
area_by_eez <- zonal(suitable_area, eez_rast, fun = 'sum', na.rm = TRUE)

# Rename the column name that zonal() automatically makes
area_by_eez <- area_by_eez |> 
  rename(suitable_area_km2 = lyr1)
```

The region with the largest total suitable area is Central CA at about 4,373 km², then Southern CA (3,329 km²), Washington (3,091 km²), Oregon (1,395 km²), and lastly, Northern CA (323 km²). When looking at just states, it's clear that California has the most suitable area for oysters. 

To keep track of the suitable area total, I join the results back to the EEZ data frame on the `rgn` column. 

```{r}
# Join the results back to the EEZ sf object
eez_suitable <- left_join(eez, area_by_eez, by = 'rgn')
```



## Map It

The data wrangling and cleaning is done, so now I can map the final product. 

```{r}
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 9

tm_shape(eez_suitable) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "suitable_area_km2",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_continuous(values = "brewer.blues", 
                                              values.range = c(0.25, 1)),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Suitable area (sq. km)",
                                      title.size = 0.7,
                                      text.size = 0.6,
                                      reverse = TRUE),
              col = "white", 
              lwd = 0.5) +
  tm_text("rgn", size = 0.55, col = "white") + 
  tm_title("Suitable Area for Oyster\nAquaculture by West Coast EEZ", size = 0.9) +
  tm_graticules(col = "gray90", lwd = 0.5) +
  tm_compass(position = c("left", "bottom"), size = 1.5) +
  tm_scalebar(breaks = c(0, 100, 200, 300, 400), text.size = 0.6, 
              position = c("left", "bottom"))
```

The map above represents the suitable area in km² for oyster aquaculture grouped by West Coast EEZs. The darker the color, the more suitable area. Vice versa for the lighter blue. Each EEZ is labelled with its respective region. You can clearly see which regions have more or less suitable area for aquaculture. 


## Turn it into a Function

To do these same steps for a different species involved in aquaculture, a function can be made. This allows for a quicker, reproducible workflow that can be applied to any species. 

```{r}
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 9

suitability_map <- function(min_sst, max_sst, min_depth, max_depth, species_name) {

  # ---- Check the inputs ----
  if (min_sst >= max_sst) stop("min_sst must be less than max_sst.")
  if (min_depth >= max_depth) stop("min_depth must be less than max_depth.")
  if (min_depth < 0 | max_depth < 0) {
    stop("Enter depths as positive meters below sea level (e.g., 0 and 70).")
  }

  # ---- Step 2: find suitable cells ----
  # Reclassify SST: 1 = suitable, NA = not suitable
  rcl_sst <- matrix(c(-Inf, min_sst, NA,
                      min_sst, max_sst, 1,
                      max_sst, Inf, NA),
                    ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE)
  sst_suit <- classify(sst_mean_c, rcl_sst, include.lowest = TRUE)

  # Reclassify depth. GEBCO depths are negative, so flip the signs
  rcl_depth <- matrix(c(-Inf, -max_depth, NA,
                        -max_depth, -min_depth, 1,
                        -min_depth, Inf, NA),
                      ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE)
  depth_suit <- classify(depth_resamp, rcl_depth, include.lowest = TRUE)

  # Keep only cells suitable for both SST and depth
  suitable <- lapp(c(sst_suit, depth_suit), fun = function(x, y) {x * y})

  # ---- Step 3: suitable area per EEZ ----
  eez_rast <- rasterize(eez, suitable, field = "rgn")
  suitable_eez <- mask(suitable, eez_rast)
  suitable_area <- suitable_eez * cellSize(suitable_eez, unit = "km")

  area_by_eez <- zonal(suitable_area, eez_rast, fun = "sum", na.rm = TRUE) |> 
    rename(suitable_area_km2 = lyr1)

  eez_suitable <- left_join(eez, area_by_eez, by = "rgn")

  # Sanity check: suitable area can't be bigger than the region itself
  if (any(eez_suitable$suitable_area_km2 > eez_suitable$area_km2, na.rm = TRUE)) {
    stop("Suitable area exceeds total EEZ area. Check the calculation.")
  }

  # ---- Step 4: map ----
  tm_shape(eez_suitable) +
    tm_polygons(fill = "suitable_area_km2",
                fill.scale = tm_scale_continuous(values = "brewer.blues",
                                                 values.range = c(0.25, 1)),
                fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Suitable area (sq. km)",
                                        title.size = 0.7,
                                        text.size = 0.6,
                                        reverse = TRUE),
                col = "white",
                lwd = 0.5) +
    tm_text("rgn", size = 0.55, col = "white") +
    tm_title(paste0("Suitable Area for ", species_name,
                    "\nAquaculture by West Coast EEZ"),
             size = 0.9) +
    tm_graticules(col = "gray80", lwd = 0.5) +
    tm_compass(position = c("left", "bottom"), size = 1.5) +
    tm_scalebar(breaks = c(0, 100, 200, 300, 400), text.size = 0.6,
                position = c("left", "bottom"))
}
```

To check if the function works, I will try it with the oysters information. Then, I can check it with my work from earlier. 

```{r}
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 9

# Oysters: 11–30°C, 0–70 m
suitability_map(min_sst = 11, max_sst = 30,
                min_depth = 0, max_depth = 70,
                species_name = "Oysters")
```

The oyster map is the same as the one I made from before, so the function works as intended. Now, I can use it on the aquaculture species of my choosing, red abalone. 

```{r}
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 9

# Red abalone: 8–18°C, 0–24 m (SeaLifeBase)
suitability_map(min_sst = 8, max_sst = 18,
                min_depth = 0, max_depth = 24,
                species_name = "Red Abalone")
```

The red abalone map is a lot lighter than the oysters map. The lighter colors means that red abalone has less suitable area. They require cooler water and have a smaller depth range that they can be grown in. Harsher requirements means that there's going to be less suitable area. Washington has a lot of suitable area since it's dark blue. The other EEZs are on the lighter side of blue, but the next EEZ that has suitable area is Central CA, then Oregon, then Southern CA, and finally Northern CA. 


## Conclusion

This analysis built a reproducible workflow to identify which West Coast EEZs have the most suitable area for marine aquaculture based on sea surface temperature and depth. For oysters (11–30°C, 0–70 m), Central California had the most suitable area (about 4,373 km²), followed by Southern California (3,329 km²), Washington (3,091 km²), Oregon (1,395 km²), and Northern California (323 km²). Red abalone had less suitable area overall because of its narrower requirements (8–18°C, 0–24 m). Unlike oysters, Washington ranked highest for red abalone, followed by Central California, Oregon, Southern California, and Northern California. This shift makes sense because red abalone needs cooler water, which favors the northern EEZs, while warmer southern waters more often exceed its 18°C limit. Northern California ranked last for both species, likely because its narrow continental shelf leaves little shallow water near the coast. Turning the workflow into a function made it easy to compare species and confirm the results, since the function reproduced the original oyster map exactly.

These results are a starting point, not a final site recommendation. The model only considers mean annual SST and depth. It doesn't account for seasonal temperature extremes or marine heatwaves, nutrient availability, substrate type, or competing ocean uses like shipping lanes and marine protected areas, which Gentry et al. (2017) include as constraints in their global analysis. SST is also a surface measurement, while red abalone live on the seafloor, so bottom temperatures may differ. Finally, the roughly 4.6 km raster resolution is coarse compared to the narrow shallow coastal zone, which may over- or underestimate suitable area along the shoreline. Adding these factors and higher-resolution data would make the rankings more useful for real aquaculture planning.
